title: Ayin
hook: ayin is an eye, and silent

segments.voice: Yesterday, samech, Moses leaning both hands on Joshua. Your line was samech supports. Who got both hands from you? Today, the end of a week of letters, and a letter that watches. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

A young woman runs away into the desert. Her name is Hagar. She is a servant in Abraham's household, pregnant, and treated so harshly that she flees. The text finds her alone by a spring of water on the road to Shur. And there an angel of the Lord finds her too, and asks a question that's almost too simple: where have you come from, and where are you going? She answers honestly. She's running. Then Hagar, the outsider, the servant, does something bold. She gives God a name. Today's letter is in it.
screen: `HAGAR RUNS INTO THE DESERT.` → `FOUND BY A SPRING.` → `SHE NAMES GOD.`

segments.voice: Ayin. In Hebrew the word ayin means an eye. It also means a spring of water, the place where water wells up out of the ground. So when the text says the angel found Hagar by a spring, in Hebrew it says by the ayin of water. There are four things to see in it. First, the eye. Hagar calls God El Roi, which the old Jewish Publication Society translation renders a God of seeing. Then she asks, in wonder, whether she has really seen the one who sees her. The runaway in the desert is not invisible. Someone has looked at her with care. Second, the spring. The place gets a name too, a well named for the living one who sees. An eye and a spring share a word, and some readers hear why: both are places where something rises up from deep inside. Third, the silence. In everyday Israeli speech today, ayin usually makes no sound at all. You write it, and the vowel carries the voice. Some Jewish communities, from Yemen and elsewhere, still sound it deep in the throat. Either way, it's a letter that can be present without making noise, a little like a good eye. Fourth, a good eye. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students to go and see the good way a person should hold to. One answers: a good eye. Ayin tovah. A way of looking at people that wishes them well. So this week ran from yud to ayin: the smallest letter, an open palm, a teacher's tall lamed, water, a fall and a lift, a hand on a shoulder. And now an eye that notices without needing to be heard.
screen: `AYIN: AN EYE, AND A SPRING.` · `HAGAR: A GOD OF SEEING.` · `A LETTER THAT MAKES NO SOUND.` · `AYIN TOVAH: A GOOD EYE.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SEES ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at someone with care. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes rest, open or closed. Bring to mind one person you see every day but rarely really look at. The neighbor, the person at the register, the one across the table. Picture their face as clearly as you can. Notice one thing about them you've never noticed before. Then try a good eye: wish them one good thing, without saying a word. If you pray, you can bring them into it. The bell holds the time.
Ayin. An eye, and a spring of water. A letter often silent, and the first letter of ayin tovah, a good eye. Today's word.
Your line: ayin is an eye. Today, really look at the person you named, and let them feel seen, even if you say nothing. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Jewish children learning the alef-bet are taught that ayin means an eye; the idea of ayin tovah, a good and generous eye toward others, is taught from Pirkei Avot.

trapdoor: what you thought: ayin is a silent letter, nothing more.
what it means: ayin is an eye and a spring; Hagar meets the God who sees her by the ayin of water.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 16:7–14 — El Roi and Beer-lahai-roi — and Avot 2:9's ayin tovah, a good eye.

notes: Genesis 16:13 paraphrased; 'a God of seeing' is given as the JPS 1917 rendering of El Roi but not quoted as a sourced quotation. Confirm the wording.
The hook says Hagar gives God a name (16:13) and avoids any 'first person to name God' claim.
Pronunciation of ayin: 'usually makes no sound in everyday Israeli speech; some communities, from Yemen and elsewhere, still sound it in the throat.' Confirm.
The link between eye and spring ('both places where something rises from inside') is attributed to 'some readers' as homiletic, not an etymology.
Avot 2:9 (Rabbi Eliezer answers 'a good eye') paraphrased; numbering varies by edition (2:9 or 2:13).
Week-end look-back names the week's letters yud through ayin (days 1338–1344) from the index.
